hypothesis: The lifetime job quota is gone, declarations are admitted and refused at each capacity, graphs register at run time, and per-slot sizing shrinks the pool use.
conclusion: Host cases pass. Case 26 of checks/os-npu-service.py: a session whose jobs field is 1 runs 120,000 jobs through the real wrapper, runtime and service without failing, and the same wrapper with the quota restored fails the case. Case 27: refusal at each capacity the arrays reach (a missing declaration, slots, depth, graphs, the image's needs and tables, a damaged graph, the pool), and fields beyond 255 admitted by tables that hold them. The device address space and page-table limits cannot be reached with eight slots and graphs of at most NBG_MODEL_MAX_BYTES (256 MiB, so at most about 2 GiB of constant regions plus the tensors); their codes are in place for when the arrays grow. Case 29: an unseen graph registered after the scheduler started and run, a damaged graph and a third beyond capacity refused, a changed copy refused at LOAD; the graph case of the mailbox check (apps/npu-sdk/host-check.c). Case 30 of checks/os-npu-graphs.py: with the eight single-operation graphs of the host set the slot regions take 258,048 bytes against 360,448 with one size for all slots.

hypothesis: An image with models supplied from a runner input region starts within the one second the secondary cores wait, and loads its resident graphs after the scheduler starts.
conclusion: Measured: 18 graphs of 0.85 to 1.1 MB (15.3 MB in all) start in the one second and load in well under the six seconds the application waits for the ring. Eighteen compiled graphs run resident through the EL0 queue (port 3-3, 852 MHz, 800 mV, Cortex-A55 at 1794 MHz); one pass over the 18 jobs takes 22.75 ms; every output equals the simulator byte for byte.
narrative: Prepare does not hash a model that carries its digest, because hashing megabytes before the scheduler would outlast the one second that the secondary cores wait for the primary core (platform/a733-smp-cached/continue.c, exit status 3, detail 0x203). A graph's layout takes tens of milliseconds on a Cortex-A55 at the boot clock; the sizing pass and per-slot sizing were folded into prepare. Two operating-system faults appeared with the longer start: the CPU clock owner's entry guard read a busy clock lease registry (a try-lock) as a refusal and ended the session, and the terminal sequence of the normal return parked unless the NPU pool was exactly 8 MiB at 0x47400000. Pool of 22 MiB placed below the monitor interval, one slot per graph.

hypothesis: A network compiled as 18 graphs runs as a chain on the CPU-rescaled queue within a few tens of milliseconds.
conclusion: Measured for 18 graphs of 92 frames (16 attention layers between a convolutional subsampling and a linear head), Cortex-A55 at 1794 MHz, NPU at 852 MHz: 24.63 ms per chain, of which 23.19 ms for the 18 jobs one after another with the SDK handshake (the batch without the handshake takes 22.75 ms), 1.10 ms for the 17 rescales and 0.32 ms for the decode.
narrative:
A network compiled as several graphs runs as a chain: graph g takes the output of graph g - 1 as its first input. Each graph
has its own fixed-point position for its input and output (16-bit dynamic fixed point), so the application rescales between
two graphs: code o at position f_out becomes code round(o * 2^(f_in - f_out)) at position f_in, clamped to 16 bits. The
rescale runs on the CPU (a shift for each element); a graph that did it would cost a job. The application of the chain
study (`apps/npu-graphs`, `NPU_GRAPHS_CHAIN`; the format of its data region is `chain.h`) registers a handle for every
graph, writes the first graph's input, submits graph after graph, reads each output once the job and its cache
maintenance are done, rescales it into the next input, and takes one greedy token for each frame of the last output. For the
